items.name: Smart Hospital Edge AI on FPGA
items.summary: Real-time ECG anomaly detection: a 1D CNN trained on MIT-BIH, quantized to INT8 (4× smaller), and run as Verilog RTL on a Xilinx Zynq-7020 with an FSM-based inference engine at 100 MHz. Fully on-device and privacy-focused.
items.quote: Heart monitoring that never leaves the device: a neural network small enough to live in silicon, and fast enough to keep pace with every heartbeat.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A real-time ECG anomaly detector that runs entirely on an FPGA. Instead of streaming a patient's heartbeat to a server, the signal is analyzed right where it's captured, so it keeps working without a network connection and sensitive health data never has to leave the device.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: The model: a 1D convolutional neural network trained on MIT-BIH, the standard collection of annotated ECG recordings used to benchmark heartbeat classification.

The squeeze: a custom PyTorch → INT8 quantization pipeline turns 32-bit floating-point weights into 8-bit integers, making the model 4× smaller and turning expensive floating-point math into cheap integer multiplies.
The silicon: the network runs as Verilog RTL on a Xilinx Zynq-7020, driven by a deterministic, state-machine-based multiply-accumulate (MAC) inference engine clocked at 100 MHz.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: A deterministic hardware engine has predictable timing: every inference walks through the same sequence of steps, which is exactly what you want from a device that's watching for anomalies in real time. Running on-device means no cloud bill, no network latency, and no patient data in transit.

items.name: Behavior Intelligence Engine
items.summary: Skeleton-based fall, person-down, and loitering detection at 18.6 FPS on a laptop CPU. (Built at ApexFlo.)
items.quote: Real-time behavior recognition on an ordinary laptop CPU, reading posture instead of faces.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A privacy-first, real-time engine that recognizes human behavior in video: someone falling, a person down, and loitering. It runs at 18.6 frames per second on a laptop CPU, with no GPU at all.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: Skeletons, not pixels: the engine works from body-pose skeletons, which keeps the signal small, fast to process, and focused on how a person moves.
Fall detection: an ST-GCN (spatial-temporal graph convolutional network) treats the skeleton as a graph of joints moving through time. It scored an F1 of 0.78 on the URFD fall dataset.
One backbone, many behaviors: person-down and loitering detection are rule-based and share the same skeleton backbone, so adding a behavior doesn't mean adding another heavy model.
Deployment: exported to ONNX for fast CPU inference, and checked to agree with the original model on 100% of predictions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Most real-world cameras aren't attached to a GPU. An engine that keeps up in real time on commodity hardware, and that reasons about posture rather than identity, is one that can actually be deployed where it's needed.

items.name: Hermathena
items.summary: LLM-driven IT service management with an event-sourced backend. (Built at ApexFlo.)
items.quote: IT support that starts with a conversation, not a form.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: An AI-powered IT service management platform. Instead of making people hunt through static ticket forms, a natural-language, LLM-driven intake assistant takes the request in plain words.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: Conversational intake: the assistant replaces the ticket form, and each request then flows through classification, SLA tracking and closure.
A backend that never forgets: an append-only, event-sourced Python/FastAPI service on PostgreSQL, so every change to a ticket is recorded as an event and history is never overwritten.
Permissions where they count: a role-based React + TypeScript single-page app (Vite), with permissions enforced on the server across four roles.
Guardrails: every model output is validated before it reaches production.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: When an AI is in the loop, trust comes from structure. Event sourcing gives a complete audit trail of every ticket, server-side permissions mean the interface can never grant what the backend won't allow, and validated outputs keep the model honest.

items.name: PRISM
items.summary: Maternal-health clinical decision support for an ICMR project.
items.quote: A second opinion for high-risk pregnancies, built for the Medical Officers on the front line.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A full-stack clinical decision support dashboard built for a project with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), India's apex biomedical research body. It helps Medical Officers manage high-risk pregnancies.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: A clinical rules engine: typed and reusable, so guidance is consistent and every rule can be checked.
Explainable risk: the system shows why a pregnancy was flagged, not just that it was.
The whole journey: guideline-based workflows for risk assessment, diagnosis, treatment planning, monitoring and referral.
Role-based access controls who can see and do what.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: In clinical tools, an unexplained alert is an easy one to ignore. Explainable, guideline-based rules put the system's reasoning in front of the person who has to act on it.

items.name: Multimodal Agricultural Intelligence
items.summary: Multilingual RAG assistant combining agricultural documents, semantic search, and weather data for context-aware farming advice.
items.quote: Farming advice that reads the manual, checks the sky, and answers in your language.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: An AI assistant that gives context-aware farming advice by bringing together agricultural documents, semantic search and weather data, in more than one language.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: A library it can actually read: agricultural PDFs are indexed so the assistant retrieves the right passage instead of guessing.
Grounded answers: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with semantic vector search ties each answer back to real sources.
Weather-aware: weather data adds the local context that turns general guidance into today's advice.
Multilingual, so people can ask in the language they actually speak.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Good agricultural knowledge often sits in documents that are hard to search and written in a single language. Grounding answers in real sources, and adapting them to the weather, makes the advice both trustworthy and timely.

items.name: HAD-Stack
items.summary: Physics-guided adversarial training for fraud detection.
items.quote: Fraudsters adapt. So should the detector.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A research framework for fraud detection that holds up against attackers who learn its blind spots. The attacker and the defender play a leader-follower (Stackelberg) game, and instead of hand-picked settings, quantum-inspired Hamiltonians decide the attacker's budget, how hard the defender regularizes, and when the game has settled.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: 0.9948 clean AUC-ROC on 26,393 real UPI transactions, with false positives halved compared with a strong Transformer baseline (42 → 21), and still robust (AUC 0.9988) under an FGSM evasion attack. Co-authored; under review at IEEE DSAA 2026.

items.name: Heart Disease Predictor
items.summary: Logistic Regression, SVM, and Random Forest compared on the UCI dataset, with an interactive Streamlit app.
items.quote: Three classic models, one honest comparison, and an app to explore it.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A machine-learning project that compares Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines and Random Forests for predicting heart disease on the UCI heart disease dataset, wrapped in an interactive Streamlit app.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: Same data, three model families: a simple, interpretable baseline next to more flexible models, so the trade-offs are visible instead of assumed.
An interactive app: Streamlit turns the trained models into a web app where you can enter values and see a prediction.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Comparing models side by side, instead of reaching for one by default, is the habit that keeps machine-learning work honest.

items.name: E-Commerce Ecosystem
items.summary: Multi-role marketplace (customers, retailers, wholesalers): Next.js 14, TypeScript, Prisma, AI chatbot support. OOP course project.
items.quote: One marketplace, three kinds of users: customers, retailers and wholesalers.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A multi-role marketplace with separate experiences for customers, retailers and wholesalers, built for an object-oriented programming course.

sections.heading: How it works
bullets: Full-stack TypeScript: Next.js 14 for the app, with Prisma for type-safe database access.
AI chatbot support built into the experience.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Multi-role systems are where design shows: each role sees different data and has different powers, and the code has to keep those boundaries clean.

items.name: Facial Expression Recognition
items.summary: A CNN that reads seven emotions from 48×48 faces, replicating a published architecture, and a gradient attack that makes it see Happy with 100% confidence.
items.quote: Teaching a network to read faces, then showing how little it takes to fool it.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A five-person team project in two parts. First, we replicated a published convolutional neural network for facial expression recognition and trained it on FER2013. Then we turned the model against itself, using its own gradients to change what it sees.

sections.heading: The data
bullets: FER2013: 35,887 grayscale face images, 48×48 pixels each, split into 28,709 for training, 3,589 for validation and 3,589 for testing.
Seven emotions: Angry, Disgust, Fear, Happy, Sad, Surprise and Neutral.
Unbalanced classes: Happy makes up 25.0% of the images; Disgust only 1.5%.

sections.heading: The model
bullets: Architecture: replicated from a published IEEE paper ↗ (opens in a new tab): six convolutional layers with ReLU, a max-pooling layer after every two (3×3 with stride 2 for the first two, 2×2 with stride 2 for the third), two dropout layers at 0.2, then two dense layers ending in softmax. About 1.2 million parameters.

A leaner pipeline: the paper also detects and aligns faces and adds facial-landmark features from dlib. With limited compute, we trained the same layer stack without that preprocessing or feature extraction, in Keras on TensorFlow.

sections.heading: Results
bullets: 54% accuracy on the 3,589 test images, against 61.7% for the paper's full pipeline. The state-of-the-art CNN ensemble reaches 75.2%.
Easiest to read: Happy (F1 0.75) and Surprise (F1 0.70).
Hardest: Fear, caught only 20% of the time (recall 0.20), and Disgust, the rarest class (recall 0.30).
Averages: macro F1 0.49, weighted F1 0.53.

sections.heading: How to fool it
bullets: Pick a target: the class Happy.
Define the loss as the negative probability the model gives that class, L = −p(Happy), and take its gradient with respect to the input image, normalized by its standard deviation.
Climb the gradient: nudge the image one small step at a time, x ← x + 0.05 · ∇ₓ p(Happy), clipping every pixel to the valid range [0, 1].
Result: neutral faces optimized this way were classified as Happy with 100.00% confidence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The same gradients that train a model can be used to fool it. The project flags three risks: disguising emotions to spoof surveillance, manipulating emotion-based access systems such as educational AI tools and behavioral-monitoring apps, and undermining automated psychological assessments that rely on facial cues.
